paragraphs: Topic models help summarize large text collections by representing documents through a smaller set of underlying topics. This makes them useful for exploring a corpus and reducing its dimensionality. The paper addresses a gap between methods that work well in practice and methods whose behavior comes with mathematical guarantees.

The authors describe two existing approaches with different weaknesses. Methods built around maximum likelihood can be computationally efficient, but their approximations lack provable guarantees. Earlier algorithms with provable bounds face practical obstacles: they are inefficient and are not robust when their modeling assumptions are violated. The proposed algorithm aims to bring theoretical assurance and practical usefulness together.

The stated result is a topic-learning algorithm that is both provable and practical. Its outputs are reported as comparable to those of the best Markov chain Monte Carlo implementations, while computation is orders of magnitude faster. This matters because it suggests that obtaining formal guarantees need not require sacrificing the speed or output quality needed for exploratory text analysis.
icml-2013-a-practical-algorithm-for-topi.tldr: The paper presents a topic-modeling algorithm with provable guarantees and results comparable to strong MCMC implementations at orders-of-magnitude greater speed.

paragraphs: The paper studies convex optimization objectives that combine two components: a self-concordant term and a regularization term that may be nonsmooth. These components create a need for an algorithm that can use the structure of the first term while accommodating the possible lack of smoothness in the second.

The authors propose a proximal Newton framework for this setting. Their method has local quadratic convergence, meaning that sufficiently near a solution, the error can shrink at a rate governed by its square. The word local matters: the stated convergence rate describes behavior near the solution rather than promising that speed from every starting point.

The paper then applies the framework to estimating sparse precision matrices for graph learning. A carefully constructed dual formulation and an analytic choice of step size produce an algorithm that avoids both Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions. Removing these operations makes the method attractive for parallel and distributed implementation, connecting the general optimization result to a concrete computational concern in graph learning.
icml-2013-a-proximal-newton-framework-fo.tldr: A proximal Newton framework offers local quadratic convergence and a graph-learning implementation that avoids Cholesky decompositions and matrix inversions.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference approximates posterior distributions for probabilistic models trained on very large datasets. It repeatedly analyzes a subset of the data and uses the result to update model parameters. These updates follow noisy estimates of a natural gradient, so the learning rate controls how strongly each subsample influences the evolving approximation.

The difficulty is that inference can be sensitive to the learning-rate schedule. A decreasing rate usually needs to be tuned separately for each application, adding practical work to an otherwise scalable procedure. The paper introduces an adaptive learning rate that requires no tuning and uses computations the inference algorithm already performs.

The authors demonstrate the method with latent Dirichlet allocation on three large text collections. In these experiments, the adaptive rate reaches convergence faster and produces a better approximation than the best hand-tuned rates tested. The contribution therefore concerns both usability and inference quality: it removes a manual choice while improving the reported outcome in the evaluated topic-modeling applications.
icml-2013-an-adaptive-learning-rate-for-.tldr: An adaptive, tuning-free learning rate improves convergence speed and posterior approximation quality in the paper’s large-corpus topic-modeling experiments.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis identifies relationships between two sets of variables by finding suitable linear combinations of each. Kernel CCA extends the search to nonlinear relationships, but the paper identifies difficulties with interpreting its results and handling irrelevant features. The aim is to capture richer dependence while retaining projections that remain connected to the original variables.

The authors introduce two extensions based on the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion and centered kernel target alignment. Both methods seek linear projections whose resulting data pairs are maximally dependent according to their chosen criterion. The nonlinear aspect lies in how dependence is measured, while the projections themselves remain linear.

This design allows the methods to remove irrelevant features and extract combinations of features with strong associations. A simulation and an analysis of previously available recorded data illustrate these capabilities. The contribution is a way to combine nonlinear dependence assessment with a more interpretable representation, making the selected combinations of original features part of the explanation of the relationship.
icml-2013-canonical-correlation-analysis.tldr: Two CCA extensions use nonlinear dependence criteria with linear projections to identify associated feature combinations and remove irrelevant features.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter tuning searches for settings that make a learning algorithm perform well. Surrogate-based optimization supports this search by building a model of how error changes across possible settings. The paper asks how such methods can benefit from previous experiments when tuning an algorithm on new learning problems.

The motivation is that experienced practitioners can transfer useful knowledge between similar problems. An automated tuner that treats every problem independently misses that opportunity. The authors propose surrogate-based collaborative tuning, called SCoT, which combines surrogate-based ranking with optimization and incorporates past experimental knowledge while simultaneously tuning on the new problems at hand.

SCoT is demonstrated in two experiments, where it outperforms both standard tuning techniques and surrogate-based optimization conducted for a single problem. These findings support the value of sharing information across tuning tasks in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is to make prior tuning experience an input to the search procedure, rather than requiring every new problem to supply all of its own evidence.
icml-2013-collaborative-hyperparameter-t.tldr: SCoT transfers knowledge from previous experiments into collaborative hyperparameter tuning and outperforms the compared tuning methods in two experiments.

paragraphs: Multinomial logistic regression is used for classification problems with multiple possible outcomes. The paper focuses on regularized models with thousands or tens of thousands of outcomes. At that scale, the computational burden can become severe: even passing through all of the model parameters can be prohibitively expensive.

The authors propose a training method that allows the likelihood objective to be optimized in parallel. This addresses the bottleneck within the training computation itself. Its importance comes from the size of the outcome space, which can make a familiar classification model difficult to train even before considering more elaborate modeling choices.

Experiments on large-scale datasets show an order-of-magnitude reduction in training time. That result provides empirical support for using parallel optimization to make these large logistic models more practical. The paper’s stated contribution centers on computational efficiency: it offers a way to train models whose parameter scale otherwise makes ordinary optimization too costly, with the reported speed improvement demonstrated on the evaluated datasets.
icml-2013-distributed-training-of-large-.tldr: Parallel likelihood optimization reduces training time by an order of magnitude in experiments with large-scale multinomial logistic models.

paragraphs: This paper brings questionnaire responses, questionnaire text, and brain-imaging measurements into a single statistical model. These sources have different forms: answers can be ordered or categorical, question text is represented through word counts, and fMRI responses are real-valued measurements. Joint analysis needs to accommodate those differences while learning connections across the sources.

The proposed Bayesian model combines a matrix factorization based on latent binary features with sparse graphical models. It uses the von Mises distribution in a new way to infer relationships jointly across people, questions, imaging stimuli, and brain regions. The latent representation provides a shared modeling structure for these otherwise heterogeneous observations.

The authors compare the model with simpler alternatives on two real datasets. They also demonstrate prediction of a person’s brain response to visual stimuli, as measured by fMRI, from that person’s answers to classical questionnaires. This finding illustrates the practical purpose of integration: information from questionnaire responses can support predictions about a different type of measurement within the studied setting.
icml-2013-exploring-the-mind-integrating.tldr: A joint Bayesian model integrates questionnaire data and fMRI, demonstrating prediction of visual-stimulus brain responses from questionnaire answers.

paragraphs: Dropout trains neural networks while randomly setting some inputs and hidden units to zero. This encourages features to contribute independently instead of depending too strongly on particular companions. Such reduced co-adaptation often improves classification and regression, but repeatedly drawing random subsets makes the training procedure slower.

The paper examines the objective implied by dropout and replaces its repeated Monte Carlo optimization with a Gaussian approximation. Training can then sample from that approximation or integrate over it. The authors support this approximation through the central limit theorem and empirical evidence, connecting the computational shortcut to the behavior of the noise introduced by dropout.

The reported result is an order-of-magnitude speedup together with greater stability. The paper develops the approach for classification, regression, and multilayer neural networks. It also extends the technique to integrate out other noise sources and small image transformations. The broader contribution is a way to account for training-time variability through approximation, reducing the work required to repeatedly realize that variability through explicit random choices.
icml-2013-fast-dropout-training-b96d2999.tldr: A Gaussian approximation to dropout delivers a reported order-of-magnitude training speedup and greater stability.

paragraphs: Understanding how two images relate is useful for tasks such as pose estimation, action recognition, and recognizing objects despite transformations. The paper considers models that represent these relationships by projecting images into subspaces. In existing higher-order Boltzmann machines and relational autoencoders, intermediate layers act as detectors associated with particular transformations.

The authors extend a mathematical analysis to show that both images can use one shared projection. This is the weight tying described in the title: the two inputs use the same projection rather than separate ones. Under this construction, the intermediate layers encode the spectrum of transformations, providing a different interpretation of what the network represents.

The paper reports that the resulting networks are easier to tune and generalize better. The shared projection therefore matters both as a mathematical structure and as a practical modeling choice. It links the treatment of the two images while retaining a representation of their transformation relationship, with the stated findings suggesting benefits for configuring the networks and applying what they learn beyond their training examples.
icml-2013-gated-autoencoders-with-tied-i.tldr: Sharing an image projection turns intermediate representations into transformation-spectrum encoders and yields networks reported to be easier to tune and better at generalizing.

paragraphs: Ranking becomes expensive when the candidate set contains very large numbers of labels, items, or documents. A method whose running time grows linearly with that set must spend increasing effort as the collection expands. This is a practical issue in information retrieval, recommendation, and large-scale annotation.

The paper proposes a general conversion from linear-time ranking to sublinear ranking through label partitioning. It learns a partition of the input space and assigns labels to each region. These choices are learned to optimize precision at k, which measures the relevance of the top k returned results. The partitioning is therefore tied to the ranking quality that matters in the intended setting.

Experiments on large ranking and recommendation tasks show that this approach makes the original algorithm computationally tractable and can also improve performance. The contribution is more than a faster way to organize candidates: it learns the organization around the desired ranking objective. The reported results indicate that reduced computational effort can coincide with improved ranking quality in the evaluated tasks.
icml-2013-label-partitioning-for-subline.tldr: Learning input partitions and their label assignments enables sublinear ranking while sometimes improving ranking performance.

paragraphs: Large-scale online learning can consume substantial memory simply by storing model weights. This paper reduces that cost by rounding the weight vector onto a coarse set of discrete values. The rounding is randomized, making randomness part of the method used to replace conventional higher-precision storage.

Compared with standard 32-bit floating-point encodings, the authors report memory reductions exceeding 50 percent during training and reaching up to 95 percent when predicting with a fixed model, with almost no accuracy loss. They also use randomized counting to implement separate learning rates for individual coordinates, improving model quality with little extra memory.

The paper supports these techniques with regret guarantees similar to those of their exact counterparts. Its empirical evaluation also reports strong memory-versus-accuracy tradeoffs relative to standard approaches. Together, these results connect a practical storage change with both theoretical learning behavior and measured performance. The contribution is a way to preserve much of the usefulness of online learning while substantially reducing the memory needed to represent its state.
icml-2013-large-scale-learning-with-less.tldr: Randomized rounding and counting substantially reduce online-learning memory use while retaining similar regret guarantees and almost all reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning representations from unlabeled data becomes difficult when many observed patterns are irrelevant to the task. Feature selection can help, but it may struggle when useful features have not yet been constructed. The paper addresses this interdependence by treating feature learning and feature selection as parts of one generative model.

The proposed point-wise gated Boltzmann machine selects information at two levels. It selects among learned high-level features represented by hidden units, and it dynamically selects raw features represented by visible units. A gating mechanism lets the chosen subset of visible inputs vary from one example to another.

This example-specific selection allows the model to focus on task-relevant patterns while ignoring irrelevant visible inputs. In experiments across several visual recognition benchmarks, the method improves on the state of the art used for comparison. The stated findings support combining representation learning with adaptive selection: the model can build useful features while also deciding which parts of each observation should contribute to them.
icml-2013-learning-and-selecting-feature.tldr: A gated Boltzmann machine jointly learns features and selects relevant inputs for each example, improving performance on several visual recognition benchmarks.

paragraphs: Portfolio construction depends partly on understanding which assets tend to move together. Investors seek attractive expected returns while avoiding combinations that expose them to shared losses. The paper argues that ordinary correlation can miss important aspects of these connections, particularly events involving large losses, motivating a different measure of connectedness.

The authors introduce a machine-learning method that learns a connectedness matrix through unconstrained optimization. Despite using an unconstrained optimization procedure, the method ensures that the resulting matrix is positive semidefinite. This combines flexibility in learning the connections with a specific mathematical property of the final representation.

The learned matrix is then used to construct investment portfolios. The paper reports portfolios that outperform both the market and portfolios optimized for minimum variance. These findings suggest that the learned connections contain useful information for the portfolio-construction setting studied. The result concerns the demonstrated use of this matrix; it does not turn that reported outperformance into a promise about every future portfolio or market condition.
icml-2013-learning-connections-in-financ.tldr: A learned asset-connectedness matrix supports portfolios reported to outperform the market and minimum-variance portfolios.

paragraphs: The paper studies how the size of boosting updates affects the margins of the resulting classifier. Its central result is that AdaBoost and closely related methods can produce approximately maximum-margin classifiers when their chosen step sizes are multiplied by a fixed small constant. This connects a simple adjustment to a formal property of the learned classifier.

That adjustment is shrinkage: each update is made smaller than the original step-size rule would prescribe. When the original step is an optimal choice, the results provide guarantees for the shrinkage procedure used in gradient boosting. The condition on the unscaled step matters for this particular connection to the existing procedure.

The analysis also covers several other step-size choices and supports the intuition that stronger regularization of line searches improves margin guarantees. Its scope includes exponential loss and similar losses, especially logistic loss. The contribution is theoretical support for how restrained updates can shape boosting’s margin behavior, rather than merely an empirical observation that smaller steps sometimes work well.
icml-2013-margins-shrinkage-and-boosting.tldr: Scaling boosting steps by a small constant can yield approximately maximum-margin classifiers, providing theoretical support for shrinkage.

paragraphs: The paper studies musical influence using topic-modeling tools, bringing a data-driven approach to a question often explored by scholars and critics. Its dataset contains 24,941 songs by 9,222 artists spanning 1922 to 2010. The learned models provide a basis for investigating influence across this collection.

The authors assess the models against a human-curated measure of influence. They report significant correlation with that measure and clear improvement over a baseline method. This comparison matters because it connects the model’s output to an independently curated account of influence, supporting its use for further analysis of musical patterns.

Using the learned model, the authors examine how influence relates to innovation. They find no monotonic relationship: greater innovation does not consistently correspond to greater influence across the analysis. However, the most influential songs were more innovative during the early 1970s and the mid-1990s. The findings therefore suggest a relationship that varies across periods, rather than a single increasing or decreasing association between these two musical properties.
icml-2013-modeling-musical-influence-wit.tldr: Topic models align with a human-curated influence measure and reveal a nonmonotonic relationship between musical influence and innovation.

paragraphs: Biclustering looks for meaningful groupings across both sides of a data matrix. This paper focuses on matrices containing categorical values and proposes a monochromatic cost function for identifying homogeneous groups. Such a formulation is relevant to applications involving pairwise interactions, including social networks and functional groupings of biological agents.

The authors analyze the resulting optimization problem from two complementary directions. They provide a polynomial-time approximation algorithm and prove that finding an exact optimum is NP-hard. The approximation result supplies a formal guarantee for an efficiently computable solution, while the hardness result explains why exact optimization is computationally challenging in general.

The paper also develops deterministic annealing as an efficient way to address the objective, presenting it as a promising heuristic for large instances. This separates the role of the practical heuristic from the formal approximation guarantee. The overall contribution combines a specific objective for categorical biclustering, an analysis of its computational difficulty, and algorithmic approaches aimed at both theoretical assurance and practical scale.
icml-2013-monochromatic-bi-clustering-04.tldr: A monochromatic objective for categorical biclustering comes with a polynomial-time approximation algorithm, an NP-hardness result, and a promising large-instance heuristic.

paragraphs: Biclustering algorithms seek coherent groups within data, but comparing their outputs requires trustworthy evaluation measures. This paper identifies size bias as a problem in that evaluation. A score can favor certain sizes of biclusters in ways that distort a comparison, potentially leading researchers to draw the wrong conclusion about which algorithm performs better.

The authors derive theoretical corrections for all of the most popular measures considered in the paper. The purpose is to remove the identified size bias so that evaluation more faithfully reflects the quality being assessed. This addresses the measurement procedure used to compare algorithms, rather than proposing another algorithm for discovering biclusters.

The paper also introduces a corrected precision-recall space. It combines the benefits of corrected measures with the interpretability and visualization advantages of their uncorrected counterparts. Numerical experiments demonstrate the usefulness of the approach. Together, these contributions make the case that a reliable comparison needs both bias correction and a presentation that allows the resulting quality differences to be understood.
icml-2013-precision-recall-space-to-corr.tldr: The paper corrects size bias in biclustering evaluation and introduces an interpretable corrected precision-recall space.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships without manipulating variables becomes difficult when there are fewer samples than variables. The paper describes existing methods whose accuracy depends on having sufficiently many samples relative to the problem size. SADA addresses this challenge by reducing the number of variables handled together while retaining the available samples.

Its split-and-merge strategy partitions variables by finding cuts in a sparse probabilistic graphical model. Existing causal-discovery algorithms then solve the smaller subproblems, and their partial results are combined to reconstruct the full causal structure. Recursive division makes each local problem smaller, allowing the same sample collection to support more accurate local estimation.

The theoretical guarantee depends on a local sparsity condition: under that condition, SADA reduces problem scale without a significant sacrifice in accuracy. The paper also reports accurate identification when samples are substantially fewer than variables. Experiments on real datasets show improvements in scalability and accuracy when SADA is added to existing algorithms, supporting its role as a framework for extending their usable scale.
icml-2013-sada-a-general-framework-to-su.tldr: SADA uses locally sparse structure to split causal-discovery problems into smaller tasks, improving reported scalability and accuracy.

paragraphs: Neighbor embedding methods produce low-dimensional visualizations, but their quadratic computational cost makes large datasets difficult to handle. The paper shows that simply subsampling the data produces inferior results and proposes a different way to reduce the optimization cost. Its approximation lowers that cost from O(n²) to O(n log n).

The method exploits the fact that the visualization occupies only two or three dimensions. In gradient-based neighbor embedding, the update for one point can be interpreted as the combined forces exerted by other points. Nearby contributions are computed individually, while distant groups are approximated through their centers of mass.

A recursive division of the visualization space into quadrants makes these grouped contributions efficient to compute. The technique borrows the structure of approximations used for n-body force calculations and applies it to embedding optimization. The authors report substantial acceleration on medium-sized datasets and the ability to bring larger data within reach. The central benefit is cheaper optimization of the visualization through spatial aggregation of distant interactions.
icml-2013-scalable-optimization-of-neigh.tldr: Approximating distant interactions in two- or three-dimensional embedding space reduces neighbor-embedding optimization cost from O(n²) to O(n log n).

paragraphs: Interactive search guides a person toward desired items through a sequence of choices. Without personalization, finding movies, music, or books may require too many costly interactions. This paper studies repeated search, where previous interactions with the same user can inform how future searches are organized.

The authors propose sequential Bayesian search, an efficient algorithm that learns a search policy from that history. They prove Bayesian optimality for the problem they formulate. They also analyze the algorithm from a frequentist perspective and establish regret that grows sublinearly with the number of searches. This means the accumulated performance shortfall grows more slowly than the search count.

An evaluation on a real-world movie-discovery problem shows performance approaching optimality as searches accumulate. The practical significance is that repeated interaction becomes useful training information: a search system can improve the choices it presents as it gains experience with a user. The theoretical and empirical results both address this improvement over repeated searches within the paper’s setting.
icml-2013-sequential-bayesian-search-45b.tldr: Sequential Bayesian search learns from repeated user interactions, with Bayesian optimality, sublinear regret, and near-optimal movie-discovery performance as experience grows.

paragraphs: Many learning problems constrain a solution to be sparse or to have low rank. A common strategy replaces these difficult constraints with convex alternatives involving the ℓ₁ norm or nuclear norm. This paper considers situations where those norms are already separate constraints, alongside the original sparsity or rank requirement.

In that setting, the usual convex relaxation does not provide the needed way to handle both requirements. The authors derive efficient sparse projections onto the simplex and an extension of it. These projections supply an optimization operation that respects sparsity within the relevant constrained set, addressing the combined constraints directly.

The paper illustrates how to use these operations in high-dimensional quantum tomography, sparse density estimation, and portfolio selection. These applications demonstrate why retaining nonconvex constraints can be important when a convex norm constraint is already part of the problem. The contribution is an efficient computational tool for this particular constraint structure, together with examples of how it can support learning problems across several domains.
icml-2013-sparse-projections-onto-the-si.tldr: Efficient sparse simplex projections support learning problems that require nonconvex sparsity or rank constraints alongside convex norm constraints.

paragraphs: Clustering scores are often used to compare possible groupings, but their behavior can complicate choosing how many clusters to use. The minimum values of Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut are known to vary monotonically with cluster count. The paper expands the analysis beyond optimal clusterings to the full collection of clusterings ordered by refinement.

A refinement splits existing groups into smaller ones. The authors establish strict monotonicity for Sum of Squares Error under strict refinement and a corresponding strict anti-monotonicity result for Normalized Cut. They also derive bounds, dependent on the data, on the change in score between a clustering and its refinement.

These results show that restricting attention to a nested sequence, such as the output of hierarchical clustering, does not resolve the cluster-count selection problem using these functional values alone. The paper further obtains data-dependent bounds on score differences between any two clusterings. Its contribution is a clearer mathematical account of how these objectives respond to changes in grouping structure.
icml-2013-strict-monotonicity-of-sum-of-.tldr: Strict monotonicity results show why Sum of Squares Error and Normalized Cut alone cannot select cluster count even along a hierarchical clustering sequence.

paragraphs: Max-product and max-sum message passing are widely used to seek the most probable configuration in a Markov random field. Many variants exchange messages over a graph, but their updates can also be understood as optimization steps. Convergent methods such as MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S fit a block coordinate descent interpretation on a dual objective.

In this view, an update optimizes a selected block of message variables while holding the others fixed, monotonically decreasing the dual objective. The paper identifies restrictions in how existing algorithms choose those blocks. Such restrictions limit the ways a larger inference problem can be organized into updates.

The proposed unified algorithm recovers MPLP, MSD, and TRW-S when given their respective objectives and block choices. It also supports much more flexible blocks, including very large ones, and dual objectives arising from arbitrary dual decompositions. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and constructive: it places established methods in one framework and expands the choices available for designing message-passing optimization.
icml-2013-subproblem-tree-calibration-a-.tldr: A unified message-passing framework recovers several established algorithms while allowing more flexible update blocks and dual decompositions.

paragraphs: Some software concerns matter greatly during execution but occupy little source code, making them difficult for topic models to discover. The paper distinguishes these subtle topics from topics that are prominent in only a few documents. Existing focused topic models address the latter form of rarity but fail to capture topics with low presence within individual documents.

The proposed subtle topic model uses a generalized stick-breaking process as a prior over multiple topic distributions. This creates a hierarchical topic structure intended to capture rare patterns beyond the capabilities of focused topic models. Its nonstandard inference procedure exploits a relationship between the stick-breaking process and the generalized Dirichlet distribution.

Experiments show discovery of subtle cross-cutting concerns in two benchmark codebases that existing topic models do not recover. The authors also report better subtle-topic discovery on general text collections. These results support treating weak document-level presence as a distinct modeling challenge, especially when a topic’s practical importance is not reflected by how much text or code it occupies.
icml-2013-subtle-topic-models-and-discov.tldr: A hierarchical topic model discovers weakly expressed software concerns and subtle text topics that existing models struggle to identify.

paragraphs: A vector autoregressive model describes how a collection of time-varying variables depends on its past through a transition matrix. Estimating that matrix becomes challenging when the number of variables is large. This paper proposes a linear-programming approach under the assumption that the observations come from a stationary Gaussian VAR process.

The theoretical analysis allows both the sample count and the number of variables to increase. Within this doubly asymptotic framework, the authors provide explicit convergence rates for the estimated transition matrix under different matrix norms. They show that the transition matrix’s spectral norm plays a central role in determining those rates.

Experiments on synthetic data and real stock data demonstrate the method’s effectiveness relative to existing approaches. The combination of estimation procedure and convergence analysis matters because it addresses growing dimensionality explicitly, rather than treating the number of variables as fixed. The paper also identifies finance, genomics, and brain imaging as application areas where high-dimensional time-series estimation can be relevant.
icml-2013-transition-matrix-estimation-i.tldr: A linear-programming estimator for stationary Gaussian VAR models has explicit high-dimensional convergence rates shaped by the transition matrix’s spectral norm.
